summaries.Q2808698: A cube 72 metres on each side wrapped in a concrete lattice, designed by Rudy Ricciotti and linked to Fort Saint-Jean by a 130-metre footbridge: inaugurated on 7 June 2013, while Marseille was European Capital of Culture, the Mucem is the first French national museum devoted to the cultures of Europe and the Mediterranean.
summaries.Q83013: Heir to Marseille's first true museum, opened in 1804 in the chapel of the Bernardines, it has occupied a wing of the Palais Longchamp, built to commemorate the arrival of the waters of the Durance, since 1873. Its collections include Rubens, Pierre Puget and Rodin's Meditation, given to the museum by the artist himself.
summaries.Q3086101: This private mansion of 1694, built for a company specialising in coral fishing off the coast of Tunisia, was bequeathed to the city in 1916 by the marble merchant Jules Cantini. It houses one of the most important public collections in provincial France for the period 1900-1980: Matisse, Signac, Kandinsky, Miró.
summaries.Q3329666: Work on the Centre Bourse, begun in 1967, uncovered Greek, Roman and medieval remains: the museum was created in 1983 to display them, together with the site of the ancient port. Reopened in 2013, it is the largest museum of urban history in France; its exhibits include wrecks of ancient ships, two of them Greek, from the late 6th century BC.
summaries.Q3330887: Founded in 1819, the natural history museum has occupied the right wing of the Palais Longchamp since 1869. Among its 83,000 animal specimens, a surprise: in 1986, a specimen of Delcourt's giant gecko was found in its collections, the very one used to describe the species.
summaries.Q1795927: On the first floor of the Vieille Charité, its Egyptian collection comes mostly from Doctor Clot-Bey, founder of the medical school in Egypt, and was acquired by the city for a derisory price. On display are a papyrus of the Book of the Dead 5.64 metres long and the four stelae of General Kasa, a set unique in the world.
summaries.Q3329184: Facing the Palais Longchamp, this private mansion of 1873 holds more than seven thousand pieces gathered across Europe by Marie, daughter of the wealthy Alexandre Labadié, and Louis Grobet, her music teacher who became her second husband. Given to the city in 1919 and opened to the public in 1926, the museum has been closed since 2020, apart from occasional openings.
summaries.Q36191617: The port's former sanitary station, built by Fernand Pouillon, became a museum in 2013: 850 works assembled by private patrons celebrate the artistic heritage of Marseille, Provence and the Mediterranean. The fumigation room, preserved in its original state, recalls the building's first life.
summaries.Q15138574: Its 40-metre cantilever, the longest inhabited cantilever in the world, has earned it the nicknames of white elephant and stapler. Inaugurated in 2013 to plans by Stefano Boeri and criticised for its cost and usefulness, the building closed in 2018 before finding its purpose in 2022: housing the replica of the Cosquer cave.
summaries.Q251672: Louis Borély had this neoclassical château built; its facade, designed by Charles-Louis Clérisseau in 1767, was simplified by the architect Marie-Joseph Peyre. Bought by the city in 1860 and listed as a historic monument in 1936, the bastide has housed the Museum of Decorative Arts, Faience and Fashion since Marseille-Provence 2013.
summaries.Q3087629: In the former Belle de Mai tobacco factory, closed by Seita, an association moved into 45,000 m2 of space as early as 1992. More than sixty artistic organisations live there today, along with a skatepark, a nursery and radio stations; in 2013, the year Marseille was European Capital of Culture, 500,000 visitors explored the site.
summaries.Q2832096: A café-concert in Moorish fantasy style inspired by the Alhambra, the Alcazar opened in 1857: 2,000 people could drink and smoke there while watching the show, and the Marseille audience, famously unforgiving, saw Yves Montand make his debut on its stage. Closed in 1966 and bought by a furniture dealer, it was reborn in 2004 as a library of nearly one million documents.
summaries.Q1103949: Founded in 1702 with a Jesuit as its first director, the observatory saw its caretaker Jean-Louis Pons become assistant astronomer and discover 18 comets. Moved to the Longchamps plateau, it revealed Stephan's Quintet there; merged in 2000, it is now the Laboratoire d'astrophysique de Marseille.
summaries.Q975925: From its limestone outcrop 149 metres high, the Bonne Mère has watched over sailors since the Middle Ages: a first chapel was built there in 1214. The present basilica, consecrated in 1864 on the foundations of a fort built by Francis I, is the work of a Protestant architect, Henri-Jacques Espérandieu; its gilded copper Virgin stands 11.2 metres tall.
summaries.Q1419757: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte laid its first stone in 1852; construction took 40 years. 142 metres long, with a dome rising to 70 metres and room for 3,000 worshippers: the Major, with its alternating green and white stone, is considered one of the largest cathedrals built since the Middle Ages.
summaries.Q3585889: Condemned in 1852 to make way for the new cathedral, the old Romanesque Major, built in the 12th century in pink stone from La Couronne, was saved from total destruction by the protests of 1853: only the choir and one bay remain. Its site once held the largest baptistery in Provence, 22 metres in interior diameter.
summaries.Q1858504: Founded in the 5th century by John Cassian near the tombs of the martyrs of Marseille, the abbey's influence extended across all of Provence: 440 churches and priories depended on it in the diocese of Marseille alone in the 11th and 12th centuries, and one of its abbots, Guillaume de Grimoard, became pope in 1362 under the name Urban V.
summaries.Q950637: Its first stone was laid in 1920, for the second centenary of the vow made by Belsunce during the plague of 1720; the building also serves as a memorial of the First World War. Construction took 27 years and the spire planned at 62 metres was abandoned for lack of funds; consecrated in 1947, the church became a minor basilica in 1997.
summaries.Q3584646: The people of Marseille call it the église des Réformés, in memory of a former chapel of the Reformed Augustinians. Begun in 1855 and inaugurated in 1886 thanks to three million francs raised through the charity of its parishioners, this neo-Gothic church with 76-metre spires was never truly finished: its facade is still waiting for its sculptures.
summaries.Q3115133: Inaugurated in 1864 on rue Breteuil to plans by Nathan Salomon, the great synagogue seats 1,200 in a Romano-Byzantine style. An organ from 1900, still in working order, continues to accompany weddings; since 2018 it has borne the name Beth Yossef, in homage to Chief Rabbi Joseph Haïm Sitruk.
summaries.Q3580413: Rebuilt from 1823 and consecrated in 1824, this neoclassical church welcomed Frédéric Chopin in 1839, who came to play the organ for the funeral of his friend the singer Adolphe Nourrit. The composer's verdict to the parish priest: "This organ is worthless, sell it". The instrument was sold on to the town of Eyguières.
summaries.Q3581149: Founded by the preaching friars of the order of Saint Dominic, the church was begun in 1526 but not consecrated until 1619. Its baroque facade of 1739, by Joseph Gérard and Antoine Duparc, was cut back in 1926: weakened by the cutting through of rue de la République, part of it was demolished as an economy measure, pediment and fire pots included.
summaries.Q1764669: Built in pink stone from Cap Couronne in the late 12th or early 13th century, this church in Provençal Romanesque style is the parish of Marseille's fishermen and seafarers. In 1943, it escaped the dynamiting of the old quarters by the German occupiers; its parish priest tolled the bell throughout the destruction of the district.
summaries.Q970362: This medieval collegiate church was razed during the Revolution: having hosted in 1793 the assemblies of a section involved in the federalist insurrection, it suffered the punishment inflicted on the "City-without-a-Name". Only the back wall and the bell tower remain, the latter spared because its clock set the time for all work in the port and the city.
summaries.Q3585913: Having arrived at Les Aygalades around 1238, the Carmelites founded a convent in 1285 on the hill that bears their name; the church was rebuilt in the 17th century. In 1870, the bishop asked his clergy to donate bells for the nation: the parish priest Decanis kept his, offering the prefect instead a machine gun worth 500 francs, paid for by the parishioners.
summaries.Q16008725: A cathedral of the Armenian Apostolic Church consecrated on 25 October 1931, it follows the structure of Etchmiadzin Cathedral to plans by Aram Tahtadjian, financed largely by the Brussels businessman Vahan Khorassandjan. Since 1973, a memorial to the Armenian genocide has stood in its garden.
summaries.Q3585891: Begun in 1447 at the head of the Old Port, the Augustinian church received a roof frame cut from the timber of a decommissioned galley given by Jean de Villages, nephew of Jacques Cœur. Renamed Saint-Ferréol les Augustins in 1803, it housed the relics of Saint Louis of Anjou, returned in 1956 and then stolen in 1993.
summaries.Q3085786: Inaugurated in 1787, the Grand Théâtre was ravaged by fire on 13 November 1919, at the end of a rehearsal of Meyerbeer's L'Africaine: only the peristyle, the colonnade and the main walls survived. The architect Gaston Castel oversaw the reconstruction of an Art Deco auditorium, inaugurated on 3 December 1924 with Ernest Reyer's Sigurd.
summaries.Q2626362: This market hall of 1909 served as the fish auction until 1975, before becoming in 1981 the Théâtre national de Marseille founded by Marcel Maréchal. Too dilapidated, it kept only its facade, rebuilt identically to within about ten centimetres: the inscription "Criée libre aux poissons" can still be read there.
summaries.Q3527792: A former actor of the Grand Théâtre, Giraud Destinval, bought the chapel of the former convent of the Lyonnaises in 1800 to build this Italian-style theatre, inaugurated on 13 September 1804 under the name Théâtre Français. Renamed the Gymnase in 1834, it hosted Sarah Bernhardt as well as Jacques Brel, before closing in 2021 for renovation.
summaries.Q3527841: Built in the Augustan era in a style close to that of ancient Greek theatres, this theatre roughly 115 metres wide sleeps beneath the city: its first remains came to light during test digs in 1945, during the reconstruction of the district destroyed in 1943. Buried under the Vieux-Port secondary school, they have been listed as historic monuments since 1966.
summaries.Q248366: Marseille's main concert venue, the Dôme holds from 1,200 to 8,500 spectators depending on the configuration. Its dome, designed by the architect Denis Sloan, recalls the hull of an upturned boat, supported by an arch 27 metres high. Since its inauguration in 1994, the venue has welcomed an average of 300,000 spectators a year.
summaries.Q1905802: Louis XIV had this fort built after the Marseille rebellion, less to protect the Old Port than to be able to bombard the city and put down another urban revolt. Its name comes from the Hospitallers of Saint John of Jerusalem, established on this promontory towards the end of the 12th century. Since 2013, it has been part of the MuCEM.
summaries.Q1763231: Built from 1660 to 1664 by the Chevalier de Clerville on the orders of Louis XIV to subdue Marseille's spirit of independence, the fort failed to convince Vauban, who in 1679 saw in it "a most magnificent assemblage of everything extravagant and ridiculous that has ever passed through the heads of the worst engineers in the world".
summaries.Q1619084: This palace began as a water tower, built to celebrate the arrival of the waters of the Durance via the canal de Marseille, 85 km long. When the first stone was laid in 1839, the Duke of Orléans warned: "Laying the first stone is not hard; it is the last one that is difficult". The palace was inaugurated thirty years later, on 15 August 1869.
summaries.Q1906882: Napoleon III had this residence built for Empress Eugénie, on a site overlooking the harbour entrance. Unfinished when the Empire fell in 1870, the palace was never lived in by the imperial couple. After winning her lawsuit against the city in 1884, Eugénie gave it to Marseille, on condition that it be used for purposes of public benefit.
summaries.Q1065581: Sixty-five buildings had to be expropriated to erect this palace on the Canebière, inaugurated by Napoleon III on 10 September 1860. When the defeat at Sedan was announced, on 4 September 1870, rioters beheaded his statue in the gallery and paraded the head through the streets: a barometer now stands in its place.
summaries.Q3361012: Inaugurated on 4 November 1862 on place Montyon, this Second Empire palace, the work of the architect Auguste Martin, is entered by a flight of 25 steps and an Ionic peristyle of six columns. In the salle des pas perdus, 16 columns of red Languedoc marble stand beneath the portraits of lawgivers, from Solon to Napoleon I.
summaries.Q169369: A bastide of stone and pink brick completed in 1862 for Eugène Pastré, it became a refuge during the Second World War: Countess Lily Pastré sheltered artists and many Jews trying to leave France, including Clara Haskil. Given to the city, the Campagne Pastré housed the Museum of Faience from 1995 to 2013.
summaries.Q2109073: This is the oldest house in Marseille, built around 1535 for Louis de Cabre, second consul of the city in 1544. Spared in 1943 when the Germans destroyed the alleys on the north bank of the Old Port, it was moved in one piece in 1954: a shift of nearly 15 metres and a quarter turn to align it with the Grand-Rue.
summaries.Q3278694: Its facade covered in stones cut into points gives it its name. Erected at the end of the 16th century or the very beginning of the 17th, it is, along with the hôtel de Cabre, one of the oldest surviving houses in Marseille; oral tradition holds it to be the palace of King René. In a state of decay, it was saved from ruin in 1914 by the association Art et Charité.
summaries.Q3145471: Built between 1743 and 1747 by the Gérard brothers, this former courthouse bears the name of Jacques Daviel, a surgeon who came to Marseille during the plague of 1720. The courts sat there until 1862; spared in 1943 during the destruction of the Old Port district, it now houses annex services of the city hall.
summaries.Q3145574: Inaugurated on 15 August 1863 on the Canebière, this grand hotel built by Jean-Charles Pot offered hydraulic lifts, telephones and electric lighting. On its facade, four caryatids represent the continents: winged fish, elephant, dromedary, sphinx. On 28 February 1896, the Lumière brothers' "Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat" was screened there.
summaries.Q2422203: Built on piles on the quai du port, it has no staircase linking the ground floor, reserved for the merchants' lodge, to the first floor: access is through the building behind, originally connected by a wooden bridge. Begun in 1653 and occupied at the end of 1673, the building narrowly escaped the demolition decreed under the Revolution, saved in February 1794.
summaries.Q2186614: Founded in 1593, this former hospital in the Panier was built from 1753 to plans by Jacques Hardouin-Mansart de Sagonne, grandson of Jules Hardouin-Mansart. Napoleon III inaugurated the new Hôtel-Dieu on 15 November 1866. Since 2013, the former hospital has been a 5-star InterContinental hotel.
summaries.Q2243437: Voted in 1784 in honour of Louis XVI, taken up again in 1823 for the Duke of Angoulême's Spanish campaign, this triumphal arch was not inaugurated until 1837: with the regimes having changed, its reliefs celebrate Fleurus, Heliopolis, Marengo and Austerlitz. The people of Marseille turned it into a saying: to have a tafanari as big as the porte d'Aix.
summaries.Q6773259: Inaugurated on 11 February 1973 in the gardens of the Cathedral of the Holy Translators, this memorial to the Armenian genocide was the first of its kind in Marseille and one of the first in France. It consists of reinforced concrete stelae, a spire and a bowl in which an eternal flame is kept burning; its construction led Turkey to recall its ambassador.
summaries.Q2489442: On the corniche Kennedy, this Gateway to the East honours the dead of the Army of the Orient and the distant lands of the First World War: a bronze statue framed by a granite arch. Built to plans by the architect Gaston Castel and inaugurated on 24 April 1927, the monument has been listed as a historic monument since 2011.
summaries.Q3497575: This David in Carrara marble is a copy of Michelangelo's famous David, given by the marble merchant and sculptor Jules Cantini in 1903. More than 5 metres tall and weighing 12 tonnes, the statue has stood since 1949 near the Prado beaches, at the intersection of avenue du Prado and promenade Georges Pompidou.
summaries.Q3296411: Built at the end of the 19th century to fix the zero altitude of mainland France, it has been measuring sea level for more than 140 years, almost without interruption. Its mechanical totaliser is the only one of its kind in the world; its records show a rise 2.3 times faster over the last 35 years than during the first 100.
summaries.Q437959: Founded by the Phocaeans in 600 BC in the Lacydon inlet, this is the oldest port in Marseille. An iron chain barred its entrance: carried off as a trophy by the galleys of the King of Aragon during the sack of 1423, it is said to hang today on the wall of the cathedral of Valencia, in Spain.
summaries.Q2037477: There is nothing natural about these beaches: they were reclaimed from the sea in the late 1970s, over 20 hectares, using rubble from the construction of Marseille's two metro lines. Before that, on mistral days, the waves would drench passers-by and vehicles along the roadway.
summaries.Q2467550: This little harbour owes its name to auffe, a plant used to make ropes and fishing nets: auffe workers settled here around 1750. On either side of the bridge that spans it stand some fifty small fishermen's houses and around 80 boat moorings, including a few typical pointus, whose catch is reserved for the local restaurants.
summaries.Q3231310: After the plague of 1720, Catalan fishermen settled in the Saint-Lambert cove, near the old infirmaries that had been left abandoned: their name stayed with the district. In 1790, the fleet numbered 75 boats and 400 fishermen. It is from this cove that Dumas has Mercédès come, the fiancée of Edmond Dantès in The Count of Monte Cristo.
summaries.Q1065573: Built in 1855 north of the Joliette esplanade, which marks the entrance to the basins of the Grand Port Maritime de Marseille, this lighthouse is a cylindrical limestone turret 21 metres high set on a keeper's house. Electrified in 1922, it is now extinguished: the red light installed at its foot has taken over.
summaries.Q2269718: This is one of the calanques most popular with the people of Marseille, and one of the few that are inhabited: it holds about a hundred cabanons and a small harbour protected by a breakwater. The cabanons are passed down from generation to generation; in 1992, their occupants joined together to limit development of the site.
summaries.Q2933592: At the very end of the coast road, past the village of Les Goudes, this calanque takes its name from the Provençal cala lònga, the long cove. In the 1960s, a téléscaphe, a sort of underwater cable car, linked it to Les Goudes: the wheel mechanisms that drove the cabins forward can still be seen.
summaries.Q2933594: Very modest in size, this calanque takes its name from the Marseilleveyre massif, of which it is the third calanque between Marseille and Cassis. It is much prized for its unobstructed view of the island of Riou.
summaries.Q3593057: Louis XIV had a small fort built here, completed in 1703, to protect Marseille's southern flank. When the army parted with it in 1914, the island passed to the Marseille industrialist André Lavai, who gave it to his future wife, the music-hall star Liane Degaby: the fort became a fashionable society haunt, and the island kept her name.
summaries.Q597747: Laid out by the landscape designer Adolphe Alphand on the former estate of the Borély family, this 17-hectare park was inaugurated in 1864. In 1910, it hosted the first aviation fortnight and the first flight over Marseille by an aeroplane; since 1962, the Mondial la Marseillaise à pétanque has brought nearly 13,000 players together there.
summaries.Q2172329: In 1967, work on the Centre Bourse uncovered the ancient port of Marseille: Greek fortifications, Roman quays preserved over 180 metres, and even a 23-metre boat abandoned around the 3rd century, preserved by the mud and then extracted thanks to freeze-drying. The garden, opened in 1983, is part of the Marseille history museum.
summaries.Q2204151: Laid out on the site of the former Prado railway station and inaugurated on 23 June 2001, this 10-hectare park celebrates the twenty-six centuries that have passed since the founding of Massalia by the Greeks. In the shade of its tree of Hope, the names of 500,000 Marseille donors are inscribed in the ground.
summaries.Q6159688: Inaugurated in 1918 and named after the Marseille botanist Édouard Marie Heckel, this garden in the parc Borély grows around 3000 species spread across nine themed gardens. Its tropical greenhouse of wrought iron and glass, built in 1870 for the Noilly-Prat family in the Gard, only reached Marseille in 1982.
summaries.Q3162496: Commissioned at the end of the 17th century by the Magalon brothers, wealthy merchants, this bastide, whose plans are traditionally attributed to Pierre Puget, was sold in 1721, unfinished, because of the plague epidemic. Its classical garden, redesigned in the early 20th century by Edouard André, is now a public park.
summaries.Q58172041: On an empty space left by the American bombing raids of May 1944, this corner of Belsunce was long the place des Chibanis, where elderly immigrant workers used to gather. Residents put up a plaque reading "place Louise Michel", in homage to the Communard who died nearby; the City made the name official in 2018.
summaries.Q2972480: At 63 hectares, the largest cemetery in Marseille is the third largest necropolis in France after Pantin and Thiais. Blessed in 1855, it received its first burials in January 1856. Here lie Edmond Rostand, Antonin Artaud, Vincent Scotto, Gaston Defferre and the singer Gaby Deslys, whose tomb nestles in a pine grove.
summaries.Q2554649: One kilometre from the église des Réformés to the Old Port: la Canebière takes its name from the Provençal canebiera, the hemp field, a reminder of the days when Marseille was one of the world's greatest trading centres for hemp used in rope-making. Mentioned as early as 1672, it took its present form in 1927 by absorbing rue Noailles and the allées de Meilhan.
summaries.Q2426692: On the north bank of the Old Port, the Panier is the oldest part of Marseille, where the Greeks founded Massalia in 600 BC. Its name is said to come from an inn whose sign showed a basket. In 1943, the Germans expelled 30,000 inhabitants and dynamited Saint-Jean; the Panier is the only part of the old quarters to survive.
summaries.Q3001343: From 1860 to 1972, cours Julien lived to the rhythm of the central fruit and vegetable market: farmers arrived around midnight, and wholesalers sold artichokes from Tunisia and oranges from Algeria. After the market moved to Les Arnavaux, it became the district of artists and musicians; its garden was inaugurated in 1980 by Gaston Defferre.
summaries.Q1137715: Created in 1670 during the enlargement of Marseille ordered by Louis XIV, the Grand Cours, whose ordered facades are attributed to Pierre Puget, was considered one of the finest squares of baroque Europe. In 1852 it took the name of Bishop Belsunce, who had celebrated a mass there on 1 November 1720, at the height of the plague.
summaries.Q2114767: Cut through from 1862 to link the Old Port to the new port of la Joliette, the rue Impériale cost 935 houses and all or part of 61 streets. Inaugurated in 1864 and lined with Haussmann-style buildings to draw the Marseille bourgeoisie back: they never moved in. It became rue de la République in 1870.
summaries.Q3390246: This square owes its name to the Lenche family, of Corsican origin, who built a private mansion here in the 16th century; Thomas Lenche founded the Magnifique Compagnie du corail, linking North Africa to Marseille. The mansion built by the Riquetti de Mirabeau family hosted Louis XIV in 1660 and was demolished at the end of the 19th century.
summaries.Q1946506: This stepped street climbs from place de Lenche to rue Caisserie, with a fine view of the Accoules bell tower. It was once called montée de l'observatoire: in 1702, the Jesuits set up an observatory at its top in their house of Sainte-Croix, known as the college of the four languages for the oriental languages taught there.
summaries.Q2997551: This seafront boulevard runs along the Mediterranean for about 3.7 km, from Les Catalans to the Prado beaches, alongside what a Marseille saying calls the longest concrete bench in the world. At no. 174, a tide gauge installed in 1884 defined, after twelve years of observations, the zero reference altitude for France: all French levelling derives from it.
summaries.Q3389888: La Plaine is not a plain but a plateau: the Provençal "plan", meaning plateau, was frenchified the wrong way. In 1883, a 700-metre tunnel was dug beneath it for the first tramway and still serves the tramway today. On 14 November 1886, Capazza and Fondère set off from here by balloon and reached Corsica. Renamed in 1919 in memory of Jean Jaurès.
summaries.Q3389745: An obelisk, erected in 1811 for the birth of the King of Rome, first occupied the centre of the square; moved to Mazargues in 1911, it was replaced by the Cantini fountain, carved in Carrara marble by André-Joseph Allar at the request of Jules Cantini. The square owes its name to Henri-César de Castellane-Majastre, who donated the land in 1774.
summaries.Q2236149: Laid out at a right angle over 3,400 metres and 60 metres wide, it is the widest promenade in Marseille, named in 1844 after the famous Prado in Madrid. Its canopy of plane trees has been decimated by canker stain, a fungus brought from the United States in ammunition crates; the city's largest market is held here every morning.
summaries.Q3450500: Its name comes from an inn, the Logis d'Aubagne. At no. 3, the Maison Empereur, founded in 1827, is the oldest hardware shop still trading in France. On 5 November 2018, the buildings at nos. 63 and 65 collapsed, killing 8 people and revealing the dilapidated state of Marseille's housing; the small square nearby has since become place du 5-Novembre.
summaries.Q2121984: This quay on the east side of the Old Port was in turn quai des Augustins, Rousseau, Impérial, Monsieur, d'Orléans, Napoléon, de la Fraternité in 1871 and then des Belges in 1915; it became quai de la Fraternité again in 2013, the year Norman Foster's Ombrière, set six metres above the quay, began reflecting passers-by, sky and sea.
summaries.Q3448887: This street in the 1st arrondissement crosses la Canebière, from boulevard Charles-Nédelec to rue d'Aubagne. It recalls the mendicant order of the Capuchins, established in 1665 on land that Catherine de' Medici had bought for the building of a convent; the property became a national asset at the Revolution, and the order was expelled from it in 1791.
summaries.Q3057827: One hundred and four steps and 15.5 metres of height to link the station to boulevard d'Athènes: opened to the public in 1925, the staircase was inaugurated with great ceremony on 24 April 1927 by President Gaston Doumergue. Among its sculpted groups, The Colonies of Asia belongs to the tradition of the colonial exhibition held in Marseille in 1922.
summaries.Q16511503: Opened on 24 May 2014, this shopping centre of 210 shops financed by the English group Hammerson owes its name to its 2,600-square-metre terrace facing the Joliette and Arenc basins. Since 2021, the Thassalia marine geothermal network has heated and cooled it using the energy of the Mediterranean.
summaries.Q202150: Inaugurated on 13 June 1937, this stadium hosted cycling races, boxing with Marcel Cerdan and even baseball played by American troops at the Liberation. Left without a roof for the 1998 World Cup and nicknamed l'Enrhumeur (the cold-giver) by Rolland Courbis, it regained a cover for Euro 2016: 67,394 seats, the second largest stadium in France.
summaries.Q371217: On 8 January 1848, the first official train left the station for Arles and back: 172 kilometres in five hours, through snow and rain. Isolated on its plateau, the station was only connected to the city centre by a monumental staircase in 1925. Since 2007, the Honnorat hall has welcomed travellers beneath 24 artificial pine trees.
summaries.Q2587975: Built from 1947 to 1952 by Le Corbusier, this slab block on piles was meant to be a vertical village: 337 apartments served by interior streets, shops, a school and a running track on the roof. The people of Marseille nicknamed it la maison du fada (the madman's house); UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage site in 2016.
summaries.Q58208336: This 136-metre office tower designed by Jean Nouvel, inaugurated in October 2018, is the second tallest in Marseille after the CMA CGM tower. According to the magazine Capital, three quarters of its floor space is occupied by public bodies or groups tied to public contracts: the only private companies are Orange and Haribo.
summaries.Q3533034: Designed by Zaha Hadid as the headquarters of the shipping company CMA CGM, the tower tops out at 147 metres: Mayor Jean-Claude Gaudin asked that it not exceed Notre-Dame de la Garde and its 154 metres. Its lobby was to house the largest private aquarium in Europe, a wish of Jacques Saadé abandoned for technical precautions.
summaries.Q3033477: Built from 1858 to 1864 on the model of the London docks, these warehouses play with the calendar: seven storeys like the days of the week, 365 metres long like the days of the year, 52 doors like the weeks, four courtyards like the seasons. Closed in 1988, they reopened in 2015 and now house offices and shops.
summaries.Q15636236: An underwater cable car: inaugurated in June 1967 between Les Goudes and the calanque de Callelongue, the téléscaphe carried its passengers over five hundred metres, at a depth of about ten metres, for twelve francs. A commercial failure, it lasted only a year, owing to its high cost, political decisions and alleged accidents.
summaries.Q23787696: This bunker for German submarines, code-named Martha, left unfinished after the Allied landings of August 1944, sleeps beneath a concrete ceiling 5.50 metres thick. Too costly to destroy, it has housed a data centre since 2020; murals probably painted by German prisoners have been rediscovered there.
summaries.Q3268957: The oldest lycée in Marseille, created in 1802 as an imperial lycée in the convent of the Bernardines built in 1746. Adolphe Thiers was a pupil there, Ampère died there in 1836, and its deputy headmaster José Custódio de Faria, once imprisoned in the Château d'If, provided the basis for an episode of The Count of Monte Cristo.
summaries.Q3558775: Built in 1865 by the architect Condamin on the corniche Kennedy, this neo-Renaissance villa was the summer residence of the olive oil manufacturer Charles Gounelle. Expropriated by the Vichy regime and never returned to its owners, it was first called Vague à la mer: Valmer, by contraction.
summaries.Q3558618: Captivated by a model of a neo-Moorish house seen at the Paris Universal Exhibition, Pierre Leclerc, a wealthy master tailor from Bourges, had this oriental folly built at l'Estaque in 1906 by the Olive brothers. Opened only once, for the 1991 Heritage Days, the family never opened its doors again after the flood of visitors.
summaries.Q99194988: First a candle factory set up in 1850 at 66 chemin de Sainte-Marthe, it became a soap works in 1856: it is the oldest soap works in Marseille. It produces olive oil soaps; its cauldron building and the basement room with its seven riveted sheet-metal vats have been listed as historic monuments since 2019.
summaries.Q1065120: Begun in 1671 to plans by Pierre Puget to confine the city's poor, the Vieille Charité lines up three storeys of galleries around a chapel with an ovoid dome. Close to disappearing in the 1950s, it now houses cultural institutions of Marseille.
summaries.Q166827: A dead-end road, then nothing: Les Goudes is Marseille's end of the world. A simple shelter where fishermen caught in a squall waited for the weather to calm, the cove was industrialised in the 19th century (soda, lead, sulphur), before the stones of the dead factories ended up as cabanons.
summaries.Q12949581: A small harbour and former fishermen's cabanons now restored: Malmousque, a sub-district of Endoume, takes its name from the Provençal Malamosca, literally "bad fly", whose origin remains obscure.
summaries.Q1229951: A hamlet of fishermen and tile makers turned working-class village, l'Estaque inspired Cézanne, Braque and Renoir between 1870 and 1914. Hit by industrial collapse from the 1940s onwards and filmed by Robert Guédiguian, the district is still known for its village atmosphere.
summaries.Q622500: Built on the orders of King Francis I between 1529 and 1531 on an islet in the bay of Marseille, the Château d'If served mainly as a prison during its 400 years of use. Alexandre Dumas made it famous as the place where Edmond Dantès, a character in The Count of Monte Cristo, was held. It is reached by boat and is one of the most visited sites in the city.
summaries.Q1464953: Pomègues, Ratonneau, If and Tiboulen: four islands 1.5 km off the coast of Marseille. Long a military site closed to the public, the archipelago only opened in 1975, when mayor Gaston Defferre turned the harbour into a marina. Ferries link the Old Port to these car-free islands, home to around a hundred year-round residents.
summaries.Q2933606: Its chilly water earned it the Provençal nickname "rafrège cuou", the combined result of the mistral, the shade and cold springs. Close to shore rises the Rocher du Torpilleur, an islet that looks like a warship. Faced with overcrowding, a summer visitor quota with advance booking has been introduced; allow about an hour's walk from Luminy.
summaries.Q2933600: In 1622, the fishermen of Marseille staged a huge tuna catch here, a "madrague", for the visit of King Louis XIII. Nearby, the Cosquer cave opens 37 metres below the surface, adorned with paintings from 27,000 to 19,000 years before our era. Its entrance is sealed, but the calanque remains a starting point for hiking and climbing.
summaries.Q2971172: Marcel Pagnol bought it in 1941 to turn it into a "Cité du cinéma" and recognised there an estate he had crossed as a child: the "château de ma mère" of his Souvenirs d'enfance. Built in the 19th century in the 11th arrondissement, since 2010 it has housed the Maison des cinématographies de la Méditerranée and its 350-seat cinema.
